1. Project identity
Project title
Sustainable Species in the Arctic
Short description

SPECIES explores environmental conflicts involving humans and other species across Norway, Finland and Greenland. Bringing together anthropology, biology, ecology, genetics, technology studies and audio-visual art, the project works with local and Indigenous communities to co-create knowledge and develop more culturally sensitive and sustainable multispecies relations in the Arctic.

2. Homepage: project vision
Sustainable Species in the Arctic
Towards more sustainable multispecies futures
How can we create sustainable futures for humans and other species in a rapidly changing Arctic?

Across the Arctic, relationships between people, animals and the environment are being reshaped by climate change, conservation policies, infrastructure development and competing demands on natural resources. These changes raise fundamental questions about sustainability, Indigenous rights, traditional livelihoods and how different species can continue to live together.

Sustainable Species in the Arctic brings together researchers, local and Indigenous communities, and artists to explore seven environmental conflicts involving reindeer, king crabs, wild ducks, seals, Lapland cattle, polar bears and muskoxen across Norway, Finland and Greenland.

Working across disciplines and perspectives, we investigate how different ways of understanding and relating to animals and the environment shape environmental conflicts. Through collaborative fieldwork, interdisciplinary research and participatory workshops, we aim to co-create knowledge that supports more culturally sensitive environmental management and sustainable multispecies futures.
3. About the project
About the project

Environmental conflicts in the Arctic are rarely just disputes about wildlife or natural resources. They also concern different understandings of nature, relationships between humans and animals, cultural practices, Indigenous rights and the authority to decide how environments should be managed.

Conventional approaches to environmental management often seek to incorporate local and Indigenous knowledge into scientific and administrative frameworks. Yet this can overlook the worldviews, practices and relationships through which such knowledge is formed, while reproducing existing inequalities between communities, researchers, industry and the state.

Sustainable Species in the Arctic takes a different approach. It explores environmental conflicts through the concept of multispecies ontologies: different ways of understanding what animals, humans, landscapes and other beings are, and how they relate to one another.

The project brings these perspectives into dialogue without assuming that they can or should be reduced to a single framework. It recognises the value of scientific research alongside local and Indigenous knowledge, and investigates how these different perspectives can contribute to shared understandings and more sustainable futures.

Through interdisciplinary collaboration, participatory ethnographic fieldwork and workshops led by local and Indigenous partners, the project seeks to build alliances between science, art and communities. Together, these collaborations will identify shared goals and explore ways to address environmental conflicts while respecting cultural practices, local aspirations and Indigenous sovereignty.

Our research questions
How can we co-research environmental conflicts through different multispecies ontologies?
How can local and Indigenous knowledge work alongside research knowledge to question dominant approaches to development, resource management and conservation?

5. Research approach
This section could sit under an Our approach or How we work menu item.
How we work
Working across disciplines and perspectives

We bring together anthropology, biology, ecology, genetics, technology studies and audio-visual art, working alongside local and Indigenous communities and other stakeholders. Each case study combines approaches suited to its particular species, environmental conflict and cultural context.
Learning through collaborative fieldwork

Researchers work with local and Indigenous partners to explore the social, cultural, historical and ecological dimensions of human–animal relations. Methods include participant observation, interviews, field visits, scientific data collection, genetic sampling and drone testing, depending on the case.
Co-creating knowledge

Participatory workshops bring together community members, knowledge holders, researchers and other stakeholders. Led by local and Indigenous partners, these workshops provide opportunities to exchange knowledge, explore differences, identify common goals and discuss how research can contribute to local priorities.
Connecting knowledge to sustainability

The project seeks to develop forms of collaboration that can inform environmental management while recognising the importance of cultural practices, Indigenous sovereignty and the relationships connecting humans, animals and landscapes.

Rather than treating local and Indigenous knowledge simply as data to be incorporated into existing policy frameworks, we explore how different perspectives can reshape the questions being asked and the solutions being considered.

Norway — Sápmi
Case study 1. Reindeer: herding, technology and Sámi knowledge
Location: Kárášjohka / Karasjok, Norway
Reindeer herding is central to Sámi culture and livelihoods, but access to pastures is increasingly affected by competing land uses, environmental pressures and state management.

This case study explores how drone technology might support Sámi reindeer herding, including locating and monitoring herds, tracking migration and identifying environmental threats. It also examines how new technologies interact with traditional knowledge and relationships between generations of herders.

Working with Sámi herders, leaders and knowledge holders, researchers will jointly test and evaluate suitable drones and explore their potential contribution to sustainable herding. The project will consider how technology can support herders without disturbing reindeer or the surrounding environment.
Key themes: Reindeer herding; Sámi knowledge; drone technology; intergenerational relations; pasture access; sustainability.
Research leads named in the proposal: Vegard Nergård (UiT) and Piers Vitebsky (Cambridge)
Case study 2. King crabs: fisheries, livelihoods and global markets
King crabs: fisheries, livelihoods and global markets

King crab fishing has become a lucrative industry in Northern Norway, partly driven by demand from China. Yet the expansion of the fishery raises questions about seabed damage, ecological change and the future of local livelihoods.

This case study brings together local and Indigenous fishers, marine biologists and anthropologists to investigate how the king crab industry might be managed in ways that balance fishing, community livelihoods and sustainable marine ecosystems.

The research will also follow the crab from its source in northern Norway to restaurants and hotels in China. King crabs exported live to the Chinese market carry QR codes that can connect consumers to information about the fisher, their family and the industry's claims to sustainability.
Following this international trade reveals how Arctic marine life becomes entangled in global markets, changing ecological relationships and competing ideas about sustainability.
Key themes: Fisheries; marine ecology; Indigenous and local livelihoods; China–Arctic connections; live-animal trade; sustainable resource management.
Research leads: Richard Fraser (UiT) and Jannike Falk-Andersson (NIVA)
Finland
Case study 3. Baltic seals: hunting, tradition and changing marine relations
Location: Bothnian Bay, Finland
Baltic seals: hunting, tradition and changing marine relations

Seal hunting has been practised in the Bothnian Bay for centuries, forming part of local livelihoods and relationships with the marine environment. Yet its cultural importance and ecological dimensions remain poorly understood in some policy and management frameworks.

Regulations governing hunting and the trade in seal products, alongside the creation of nature reserves, have reshaped how local communities hunt seals, use their catch and relate to other species, including fish.

This case study investigates how different understandings of hunting, animal care and sustainability shape debates over seal management. It also examines how interruptions in the transmission of traditional knowledge have affected hunting practices and the ethical relationships through which hunting has historically been understood.

The research asks whose sustainability is being prioritised, how different species are affected, and what forms of hunting and resource management are possible under changing ecological and regulatory conditions.
Key themes: Seal hunting; traditional knowledge; hunting ethics; conservation policy; marine ecosystems; multispecies sustainability.
Research leads: Florian Stammler (University of Lapland) and Juha Kantanen (LUKE), with a postdoctoral researcher.
Case study 4. Lapland cattle: genetic heritage and Arctic resilience
Location: Finnish Lapland
Lapland cattle: genetic heritage and Arctic resilience

Northern Finncattle, known in Finnish as Lapin Lehmä, have long been part of the multispecies livelihoods of Finnish Lapland. During the twentieth century, the breed was reduced almost to extinction before a conservation programme helped restore its population.

Today, farmers are exploring new forms of sustainable agricultural production using the breed's milk, meat and other products. Its hardiness, modest feeding requirements, disease resilience and high-fat milk are valued characteristics in the Arctic environment.

This case study combines anthropological and genetic research to investigate the relationships between local narratives of resilience, cultural understandings of sustainability and the biological characteristics of the breed.

Genetic research will examine gene expression associated with the cattle's resilience and adaptation to Arctic conditions, while anthropological research will explore how these qualities are understood and valued within local communities and multispecies farming environments.
Key themes: Native breeds; genetic conservation; sustainable agriculture; resilience; local knowledge; Arctic food systems.
Research leads: Nuccio Mazzullo (University of Lapland) and Juha Kantanen (LUKE).
Greenland
Case study 6. Polar bears: predation, climate change and food security
Location: Ittoqqortoormiit, East Greenland
Polar bears: predation, climate change and food security

In Ittoqqortoormiit, encounters with hungry polar bears are becoming an increasing concern for local residents. Community members connect these encounters to thinning sea ice and changes in polar bear populations, including the effects of hunting quotas.

Polar bears have long been important as sources of food and skins in Indigenous communities. Changes in hunting opportunities, wildlife management and environmental conditions raise questions about food security, safety and the future of local hunting practices.

This case study explores changing relationships between predators and prey, including concerns that polar bears moving onto land may increasingly prey on muskoxen. Working with hunters, their families and local wildlife-management practitioners, researchers will investigate how different understandings of predation and sustainability intersect with climate change, colonial histories and geopolitical interests.
Key themes: Polar bears; climate change; hunting; predation; food security; wildlife management; human–animal relations.
Research leads: Janne Flora and Floris M. van Beest (Aarhus)
Case study 7. Muskoxen: emergent ecologies and sustainable coexistence
Location: Kangerlussuaq, West Greenland
Muskoxen: emergent ecologies and sustainable coexistence

Muskoxen were introduced to Kangerlussuaq in West Greenland in the 1960s. Since then, the population has grown, contributing to the development of a substantial hunting industry and creating new ecological relationships between people, animals and the landscape.

This changing environment raises questions about how humans and animals adapt not only to their surroundings but also to one another. How do unfamiliar ecological arrangements become established, durable and liveable? And what kinds of knowledge and management practices can support sustainable coexistence?

The research combines anthropological and ecological perspectives to investigate how muskoxen become part of changing multispecies communities and how wildlife management can respond to new ecological conditions.

Working with Indigenous hunters, the project will also develop a modelling tool to explore hypothetical harvesting scenarios, helping assess strategies that consider both conservation objectives and the needs of multiple species.
Key themes: Muskoxen; ecological change; introduced species; hunting; wildlife management; modelling; multispecies coexistence.
Research leads: Astrid Oberborbeck Andersen (Aalborg University) and Niels Martin Schmidt (Aarhus), with a PhD researcher.
7. Project structure and work packages
Three regions, seven species-conflicts
The project is organised into three regional work packages.
WP1 — Sápmi, Norway
Reindeer: herding, drone technology and Sámi knowledge
King crabs: fisheries, local livelihoods and international markets
WP2 — Finland
Baltic seals: hunting traditions, regulation and marine relations
Lapland cattle: genetic heritage, resilience and sustainable agriculture
WP3 — Greenland
Polar bears: predation, climate change and food security
Muskoxen: changing ecologies and sustainable coexistence

Across all three regions, researchers and local and Indigenous partners investigate how different understandings of human–animal relations shape environmental conflicts, and how collaborative knowledge production can support more sustainable futures.
8. Interdisciplinary team and collaboration
An interdisciplinary collaboration
Sustainable Species in the Arctic brings together researchers from anthropology, biology, ecology, genetics and technology studies, alongside artists and local and Indigenous partners.

The project combines long-term ethnographic expertise with ecological research, genetic analysis, technological experimentation and artistic practice. Each case study draws on the expertise of researchers familiar with the species and its local context.

Collaboration is central to the research. Local and Indigenous partners are not simply sources of information, but active participants in framing research questions, conducting fieldwork, sharing knowledge and identifying possible solutions.

By creating opportunities for dialogue across disciplines and perspectives, the project aims to build lasting alliances between research, communities and the arts, contributing to more culturally sensitive and sustainable approaches to environmental management.
9. Expected contribution and impact
Towards sustainable multispecies futures
The project aims to advance environmental and cultural sustainability in the Arctic by bringing different forms of knowledge into dialogue.
Through interdisciplinary research and collaboration with local and Indigenous communities, we seek to:
Develop a deeper understanding of environmental conflicts and the different worldviews that shape them.
Strengthen collaboration between researchers, local communities, Indigenous knowledge holders and artists.
Identify common goals and potential solutions through participatory workshops.
Explore more culturally sensitive approaches to conservation and resource management.
Support sustainable relations between humans, animals and their environments.
Build alliances that recognise local priorities, Indigenous sovereignty and the value of different knowledge traditions.
Our ambition is not simply to resolve individual conflicts, but to explore how different perspectives can work together to shape more sustainable multispecies futures.
